Zimbabwe reels from sharp currency collapse; Unki among companies hit

HARARE, June 14 — Zimbabwe’s economy is reeling from a rapid currency collapse that has sent shockwaves through businesses and households, with companies such as Unki reporting disruptions as the local dollar plunges to record lows.

The Zimbabwean dollar lost more than 45% of its value against the U.S. dollar over the past two weeks, according to data from the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, fueling a surge in prices and widespread uncertainty. The crisis has led to shortages of imported goods and raw materials, with trading on the Harare Stock Exchange suspended twice this week amid volatility.

Unki, a major employer in the mining sector, said in a statement Friday it was “experiencing significant challenges in sourcing key inputs” due to the currency’s sharp decline. “We are working closely with suppliers and authorities to mitigate the impact on operations and jobs,” the company added.

Many other firms, including retail and manufacturing businesses, have scaled back production or suspended operations. “The exchange rate volatility is making it almost impossible to plan or price goods,” said Farai Chikore, spokesperson for the Zimbabwe Chamber of Commerce. “Companies are struggling to access foreign currency for essential imports.”

Inflation, already high, has accelerated further. Zimbabwe’s Consumer Council reports the cost of a basic food basket rose 38% in the past month. “Ordinary families are being squeezed as prices spike daily,” said council director Rosemary Ncube.

Finance Minister Mthuli Ncube told reporters the government was “monitoring the situation closely” and considering additional measures to stabilize the currency. However, analysts warned that confidence in the Zimbabwean dollar has eroded. “People are rushing to convert savings into U.S. dollars,” said independent economist Tendai Biti. “This has all the hallmarks of a deepening financial crisis.”

The currency turmoil shows no immediate signs of abating.
